questions.question: Your team edits the same configuration file and one change breaks the service. What helps the team most in that situation?
options: A version history that shows who changed what and allows going back
Keeping a single copy of the file on a shared drive with no history
Renaming the file every day with the current date
Deleting the file and rewriting it from memory
questions.explanation: A recorded history with author and message lets the team compare versions and revert the breaking change. This lesson shows how Git provides exactly that history.

questions.question: What happens when you run git checkout -b experiment/new-optimizer?
options: Git downloads a remote branch with that name
Git deletes the current branch and renames it
Git merges the branch into main
Creates and checks out that branch
questions.explanation: The -b option asks Git to create experiment/new-optimizer from the current commit and check it out immediately.

questions.question: Why should .pt, .pth, and .safetensors usually be listed in .gitignore?
options: They are large model checkpoints
Git refuses to track any binary file
They are shell scripts that need execute permission
They contain the commit history for the repository
questions.explanation: Checkpoint files can consume hundreds of megabytes or more. Ignoring them keeps source history usable; a project can publish them through dedicated artifact storage instead.

questions.question: Which command shows a compact branch graph with commit decorations?
options: git status --history --branches
git log --oneline --decorate --graph
git diff --remote --compact
git branch --commit-files
questions.explanation: git log --oneline --decorate --graph shows abbreviated commits, the parent graph, and names such as branches and tags.

questions.question: After git add ., you notice that model.pt is staged. What is the safest immediate fix?
options: git push model.pt and delete it from the remote later
git commit --amend --no-edit without changing the index
Unstage it, ignore it, and recheck status
git branch -D main
questions.explanation: Unstaging the checkpoint prevents it from entering the next commit. Adding the ignore rule and checking status prevents the same mistake on the next add.

questions.question: A teammate wants to merge an optimizer experiment without disturbing main. Which sequence best preserves an inspectable history?
options: Edit directly on main and force-push every intermediate file
Delete the experiment branch before anyone can inspect it
Copy the repository directory and never record which version was used
Use a reviewed experiment branch, then merge it
questions.explanation: An isolated branch keeps the experiment reversible. A focused commit and passing tests give collaborators something concrete to review before the merge.
